events.label: 4.5 billion years ago
events.title: Mercury forms
events.detail: Mercury formed about 4.5 billion years ago when gravity pulled gas and dust together in the inner solar nebula. Its young surface was molten.

sources.title: NASA Science: Mercury facts

events.label: ~4.5 billion years ago
events.title: Stripped mantle?
events.detail: Mercury's iron core spans about 85% of its radius, far more than any other rocky planet. One idea is that a giant impact (or a "hit-and-run" glancing collision) stripped away much of its rocky mantle; others argue the iron-rich mix was set by where and how it formed. None is settled.

sources.title: NASA Science: Mercury facts
Benz et al. 2007, The Origin of Mercury, Space Science Reviews
Asphaug & Reufer 2014, Mercury and other iron-rich bodies as relics of inefficient accretion, Nature Geoscience
Smith et al. 2012, Gravity field and internal structure of Mercury from MESSENGER, Science

events.label: ~4.4 billion years ago
events.title: Dark carbon crust
events.detail: MESSENGER found that Mercury's darkest terrain is rich in carbon, most likely graphite. Researchers interpret it as remnants of an ancient crust that floated on the cooling magma ocean, which would help explain why Mercury is so dark.

sources.title: Peplowski et al. 2016, Remote sensing evidence for an ancient carbon-bearing crust on Mercury, Nature Geoscience

events.label: 4.1–4.0 billion years ago
events.title: Heavy bombardment
events.detail: Crater statistics from MESSENGER indicate Mercury's oldest surviving terrains date to about 4.0–4.1 billion years ago: an era of intense impacts and volcanism erased anything older.

sources.title: Marchi et al. 2013, Global resurfacing of Mercury 4.0–4.1 billion years ago, Nature

events.label: ~3.9 billion years ago
events.title: Caloris impact
events.detail: An asteroid impact carved the Caloris basin, about 1,550 km across and one of the largest impact basins in the solar system. The density of craters on its floor dates it to roughly 3.8–3.9 billion years ago, late in the heavy bombardment.

sources.title: NASA Science: Mercury facts
NASA/JPL Photojournal PIA10935: Young Cunningham crater in old Caloris basin

events.label: ~3.7 billion years ago
events.title: Flood lavas
events.detail: Vast sheets of runny lava flooded Mercury's northern high latitudes, covering about 6% of the planet with smooth volcanic plains up to kilometres thick. Lava also filled the interior of Caloris.

sources.title: Head et al. 2011, Flood volcanism in the northern high latitudes of Mercury revealed by MESSENGER, Science

events.label: ~3.5 billion years ago
events.title: Lavas go quiet
events.detail: Crater-count ages of Mercury's smooth plains suggest large-scale effusive volcanism ended by about 3.5 billion years ago, as the shrinking planet squeezed shut the paths magma used to reach the surface.

sources.title: Byrne et al. 2016, Widespread effusive volcanism on Mercury likely ended by about 3.5 Ga, Geophysical Research Letters

events.label: Over ~3.9 billion years
events.title: Planet shrinks
events.detail: As its interior cooled, Mercury contracted, pushing up long cliffs (lobate scarps), some more than a kilometre high, across the globe. MESSENGER mapping implies the radius shrank by up to about 7 km.

sources.title: NASA Science: Mercury facts
Byrne et al. 2014, Mercury's global contraction much greater than earlier estimates, Nature Geoscience

events.label: Last ~50 million years
events.title: Still shrinking
events.detail: Small, crisp thrust-fault scarps seen in MESSENGER's lowest-altitude images are geologically young, under about 50 million years old, suggesting Mercury is still contracting today.

sources.title: Watters et al. 2016, Recent tectonic activity on Mercury revealed by small thrust fault scarps, Nature Geoscience

events.label: 29 March 1974
events.title: Mariner 10
events.detail: NASA's Mariner 10 made the first of three flybys of Mercury, eventually photographing about 45% of the surface and discovering its magnetic field.

sources.title: NASA Science: Mariner 10

events.label: 18 March 2011
events.title: MESSENGER arrives
events.detail: MESSENGER became the first spacecraft to orbit Mercury and went on to map the whole planet. It found bright "hollows", shallow pits that appear to form as volatile material escapes and may still be forming today.

sources.title: NASA Science: MESSENGER
Blewett et al. 2011, Hollows on Mercury: MESSENGER evidence for geologically recent volatile-related activity, Science

events.label: 29 November 2012
events.title: Polar ice
events.detail: MESSENGER confirmed that water ice is the main constituent of deposits in permanently shadowed craters near Mercury's poles, often buried under a dark layer 10–20 cm thick. The planet nearest the Sun keeps ice because its axis is barely tilted.

sources.title: Johns Hopkins APL: MESSENGER finds new evidence for water ice at Mercury's poles (2012)
Lawrence et al. 2013, Evidence for water ice near Mercury's north pole, Science

events.label: 30 April 2015
events.title: MESSENGER ends
events.detail: Out of fuel, MESSENGER was allowed to crash into Mercury's surface after more than four years in orbit, ending the mission.

sources.title: NASA Science: MESSENGER

events.label: Today
events.title: Today
events.detail: Mercury is an airless, cratered world with a vast iron core, polar ice and a surface that swings between about 430 °C by day and −180 °C by night. ESA and JAXA's BepiColombo shed its transfer module on 3 September 2026 and is closing in on orbit insertion.

sources.title: NASA Science: Mercury facts
ESA: Latest updates – BepiColombo's arrival at Mercury

events.label: 21 November 2026
events.title: BepiColombo arrives
events.detail: ESA plans to capture the joined MPO and JAXA Mio orbiters into polar orbit on 21 November 2026, release Mio on 9–10 December, and reach MPO's final science orbit in March 2027. Arrival slipped from December 2025 after a 2024 thruster power problem.

sources.title: ESA: Latest updates – BepiColombo's arrival at Mercury

events.label: Within 5 billion years
events.title: Orbital chaos?
events.detail: In 2,501 simulations of the solar system, about 1% sent Mercury's orbit so eccentric within 5 billion years that it could collide with Venus or the Sun, or destabilise the inner planets. In the other 99% it carries on as today.
events.projected_by: Jacques Laskar & Mickaël Gastineau, Nature, June 2009

sources.title: Laskar & Gastineau 2009, Existence of collisional trajectories of Mercury, Mars and Venus with the Earth, Nature

events.label: In ~7.6 billion years
events.title: Swallowed by Sun
events.detail: As the Sun swells into a red giant near the tip of its red-giant branch, about 7.6 billion years from now, models show it engulfing Mercury and Venus. The planet would be heated, vaporised and dragged inward.
events.projected_by: K.-P. Schröder & R. C. Smith, MNRAS, 2008

sources.title: Schröder & Smith 2008, Distant future of the Sun and Earth revisited, MNRAS
